name: HALLIGAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the defendant's arrest violated Payton due to constructive entry, which is also protected by the State Constitution, and that the Appellate Division applied the wrong legal standard to assess the voluntariness of the tenant's consent, requiring remittal for re-evaluation of the weapon possession charge.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Appellate Division correctly found the tenant's consent voluntary, that attenuation analysis is not applicable to a third party's consent following a Payton violation against the defendant, and that the majority's recognition of constructive Payton violations and invocation of the State Constitution are unpreserved and legally unsound.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that Newburgh, as a legislatively created political subdivision, cannot assert a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision.

name: Judge Garcia
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: Judge Halligan

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that a defendant can forfeit the constitutional right to a trial by a jury of 12 through egregious misconduct, especially when no alternate jurors are available and the misconduct affects a deliberating juror, thereby protecting the integrity of the justice system.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Article IX of the State Constitution does not expressly or implicitly limit the legislature's plenary authority to mandate the timing of certain elections, and therefore the Even Year Election Law is a proper exercise of that authority.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the State's Climate Act does not preempt local greenhouse gas emission regulations, as the Act encourages complementary local action and does not demonstrate an intent to occupy the entire field.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Act is constitutional because New York's separation of powers doctrine is flexible, the Governor's appointment and removal powers are not exclusive, and the Act serves the paramount goal of maintaining public trust by limiting executive self-regulation in ethics enforcement.

name: Judge Garcia
description: Dissented, argued that the Act unconstitutionally encroaches on executive power by creating a commission with sweeping enforcement authority, a majority of legislative appointees, and limited executive oversight, thereby violating bedrock separation of powers principles.

name: Judge Singas
description: Concurred with Judge Garcia's dissenting opinion.

name: Judge Scarpulla
description: Concurred with Judge Garcia's dissenting opinion.

name: Judge Cannataro
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that Article II, section 1 of the New York State Constitution explicitly limits voting to citizens, and this restriction cannot be superseded by local law or home rule provisions.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that Local Law 11 is consistent with the State Constitution because Article II, section 1 is an affirmative right that does not prohibit localities from expanding the franchise to noncitizens under home rule authority, but the law is void for failing to hold a public referendum.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the New York Constitution does not explicitly require in-person voting and the removal of the Election District Provision in 1966, along with the legislature's plenary power over election methods, means the Early Mail Voter Act is constitutional despite a rejected ballot initiative.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred in result, argued that while the Constitution once required in-person voting, the 1966 amendment removed that requirement, and the current text does not prohibit mail-in voting, disagreeing with the majority's historical analysis and speculation about political motives.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Constitution has long been understood to limit absentee voting to specific categories, and the legislature's attempt to pass universal mail-in voting after voters rejected a constitutional amendment to do so disregards the People's will and violates constitutional limits.

name: HALLIGAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that trial counsel was not ineffective for not requesting a cross-racial identification instruction because it was discretionary at the time and not an egregious single error.

name: WILSON, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that counsel's representation was constitutionally sufficient as the mandatory instruction rule came after the trial, and counsel did request a general eyewitness unreliability charge.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that counsel was ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification charge, as its importance was widely understood, especially in a single-witness cross-racial identification case.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the importance of cross-racial identification charges was well-recognized before Boone, making counsel's failure to request it ineffective assistance.

name: Wilson, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that counsel's failure to request the only applicable defense instruction (voluntary surrender) despite supporting testimony constituted ineffective assistance, depriving the defendant of a fair trial.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Dissented, argued that counsel was not ineffective as the defendant was not entitled to a voluntary surrender instruction, and the majority's ruling ignores facts, lacks common sense, and is dangerous as a matter of policy.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that police interference with a bicyclist is a seizure requiring reasonable suspicion or probable cause, similar to automobile stops, and the officers in this case lacked such justification.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that police encounters with bicyclists should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis, not a per se seizure, and the officers had founded suspicion to conduct a common-law inquiry.

name: Chief Judge Wilson
description: Concurred, argued that the 2014 constitutional amendments limit court-drawn maps to only what is necessary to remedy a violation of law, and therefore the IRC has a continuing constitutional duty to produce new maps for future elections.

name: Judge Cannataro
description: Dissented, argued that the court-ordered maps from Harkenrider should remain in force until the next federal decennial census, and the majority's decision rewrites the Constitution and undermines the judiciary's role in safeguarding fair elections.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Administrative Code § 10-181 is a valid exercise of the City's municipal law-making authority, as it is neither preempted by state law nor unconstitutionally vague.

name: WILSON, CHIEF JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the legislature properly delegated authority to the Commission to promulgate Familial DNA Search Regulations.

name: LINDLEY, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Commission overstepped its authority by engaging in legislative policy-making not authorized by the legislature when promulgating familial DNA search regulations.

name: Troutman

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the People's unexplained 31-month delay in a four-year pre-indictment period violated the defendant's constitutional right to prompt prosecution, requiring dismissal of the indictment.

name: GARCIA, Judge
description: Dissented, argued that the pre-indictment delay did not violate the defendant's constitutional right to a speedy trial, aligning with the Appellate Division's reasoning.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the pre-indictment delay did not violate the defendant's constitutional right to a speedy trial, as there was no discernible impact on his defense, and the majority's decision undermines justice for sexual assault victims.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the warrantless inspections authorized by the ELD rule fall within the administrative search exception to the warrant requirement and do not constitute unreasonable searches and seizures under the State Constitution.

name: CANNATARO, J.
description: Concurred, argued that Local Law No. 2 is consistent with state law and the New York Constitution, as RPTL article 11 permits cities to opt back in and does not require an agreement under RPTL 1150 for a county to enforce city taxes.

name: Judge Halligan
description: Other, took no part in the decision.

name: WILSON, CHIEF JUDGE
description: Concurred, argued that the police lacked reasonable suspicion to believe Mr. Johnson had committed a crime or was in possession of a weapon, and thus the evidence seized from the unjustified stop and frisk must be suppressed.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while agreeing with the result, the De Bour framework itself is flawed and has proven counterproductive, failing to protect individuals from subconstitutional abuses and contributing to racial profiling and dangerous escalations in police encounters.

name: Cannataro, Acting Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the enabling act is a valid assignment of power to a temporary commission with a discrete purpose and standards, and does not unconstitutionally delegate legislative power or violate separation of powers.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while the Enabling Act weakens the Governor's checks on compensation, a narrow construction and heightened judicial scrutiny allow it to pass constitutional muster.

name: SINGAS, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the Enabling Act unconstitutionally delegates core legislative power to an unelected committee, violating constitutional lawmaking procedures and the requirement that salaries be 'fixed by law'.

name: DiFIORE, Chief Judge
description: Concurred, argued that the legislature's congressional and state senate maps were procedurally and substantively unconstitutional, requiring judicial oversight for new maps.

name: TROUTMAN, J.
description: Dissented in part, argued that the court should not issue an advisory opinion on substantive gerrymandering and should order the legislature to adopt an IRC-approved plan.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that petitioners failed to prove unconstitutional gerrymandering beyond a reasonable doubt and the majority's remedy strips legislative authority.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the legislature acted within its authority and there was no procedural or substantive violation of the Constitution.

name: Judge Wilson
description: Dissented, argued that Mr. Dawson unequivocally invoked his right to counsel, and the majority's decision vitiates constitutional protections against self-incrimination and the right to due process by imposing an unrealistic linguistic burden on defendants.

name: Chief Judge DiFIORE
description: Concurred, arguing that IFS contests are skill-based competitions, not games of chance or bets/wagers, and thus do not constitute prohibited gambling under the Constitution.

name: Judge WILSON
description: Dissented, arguing that IFS contests are clearly gambling under the common understanding of the term, and the majority's decision improperly redefines gambling, thereby usurping the constitutional process and legislative authority.

name: Judge Garcia
description: Took no part in the decision.

name: GARCIA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the Right of Way Law's ordinary negligence mens rea is constitutional and not preempted by state law, citing precedents for strict liability and ordinary negligence in criminal statutes, and affirming the City's authority to enact such laws.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that while joining the majority's decision, the basis for the City's authority to criminalize traffic infractions is unclear, and the question of whether cities can criminalize violations designated as traffic infractions by the state remains unresolved.

name: Chief Judge DiFIORE
description: Concurred, argued that eavesdropping warrants are executed where law enforcement intentionally records or overhears communications, not where the target or device is located, and that this interpretation is consistent with statutory language and legislative intent, ensuring centralized oversight and protecting privacy.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the statute does not authorize a New York court to issue a warrant for calls between non-residents not present in New York, and that the majority's interpretation grants law enforcement an unreasonable, unlimited geographic reach, infringing on privacy.

name: RIVERA, J.
description: Concurred, argued that the construction of snowmobile trails requiring extensive tree cutting and land alteration violates the 'forever wild' provision of the New York State Constitution.

name: STEIN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that the project does not constitute a 'substantial change' to the Forest Preserve and that the majority misinterprets the 'Forever Wild' provision, thwarting public access and the drafters' intent.

name: WILSON, J.
description: Concurred, argued that New York law requires search warrants to particularly describe the places, vehicles, and persons to be searched, and the warrant in this case did not mention the vehicles, nor was there probable cause established for searching them.

name: FEINMAN, J.
description: Dissented, argued that a warrant authorizing the search of "entire premises" should permit the search of vehicles parked on the premises if they may contain the items authorized to be seized, treating vehicles like other containers, and that the majority's position deviates from federal and other state high court precedent.
